questions.stem: Does 'dominant' mean an allele is more common in a population?

options.text: Yes — dominant alleles are always more frequent
No — dominant means the allele is expressed in the phenotype even when only one copy is present (heterozygous); it says nothing about frequency
Yes — dominant alleles are stronger and will eventually replace recessive alleles
No — but dominant alleles are always beneficial

questions.explanation: Dominant does NOT mean more common. Dominance only describes how the allele affects the phenotype — a dominant allele is expressed even in heterozygotes. A dominant allele can be rare (e.g., Huntington's disease is caused by a dominant allele but is uncommon), and a recessive allele can be very common.

questions.stem: What is the difference between genotype and phenotype?

options.text: They mean the same thing
Genotype is the genetic makeup (alleles) of an organism; phenotype is the observable characteristics, influenced by both genotype and environment
Genotype is the physical appearance; phenotype is the genetic code
Genotype only applies to dominant traits; phenotype only to recessive

questions.explanation: Genotype refers to the combination of alleles an organism has for a particular gene (e.g., Bb). Phenotype is the observable characteristic that results (e.g., brown eyes). Phenotype is influenced by both genotype AND environmental factors. Two organisms can have different genotypes but the same phenotype (e.g., BB and Bb may both show the dominant trait).

questions.stem: What does 'homozygous' mean?

options.text: Having two different alleles for a gene
Having two identical alleles for a gene
Having only one allele for a gene
Having no alleles for a gene

questions.explanation: Homozygous means having two identical alleles for a particular gene — either homozygous dominant (e.g., BB) or homozygous recessive (e.g., bb). Heterozygous means having two different alleles (e.g., Bb).

questions.stem: Two heterozygous parents (Bb × Bb) are crossed. What is the probability of an offspring being homozygous recessive (bb)?
questions.explanation: Using a Punnett square: Bb × Bb gives offspring in the ratio 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb. The probability of homozygous recessive (bb) is 1 in 4, or 25%. Remember: these are PROBABILITIES, not guarantees. Each fertilisation event is independent, so each individual offspring has a 25% chance of being bb.

questions.stem: Does a Punnett square guarantee the exact ratio of offspring?

options.text: Yes — the ratio will always be exact
No — it shows probabilities; actual results may differ due to chance, especially with small sample sizes
Yes — but only for monohybrid crosses
No — Punnett squares are always inaccurate

questions.explanation: A Punnett square shows theoretical PROBABILITIES, not guaranteed outcomes. Each fertilisation is an independent event. With a 3:1 expected ratio, you would not expect exactly 3 dominant and 1 recessive from 4 offspring. The larger the sample size, the closer the actual ratio will be to the predicted ratio.

questions.stem: What is a test cross?

options.text: Crossing two homozygous dominant organisms
Crossing an organism with the dominant phenotype with a homozygous recessive organism to determine its genotype
Crossing two organisms of different species
Testing whether an organism is male or female

questions.explanation: A test cross involves crossing an organism showing the dominant phenotype (unknown genotype — either BB or Bb) with a homozygous recessive organism (bb). If any offspring show the recessive phenotype, the unknown parent must be heterozygous (Bb). If all offspring show the dominant phenotype, the parent is likely homozygous dominant (BB).

questions.stem: How is sex determined in humans?

options.text: By the mother's hormones during pregnancy
By the sex chromosomes: XX = female, XY = male
By the temperature during fetal development
Randomly, with no genetic basis

questions.explanation: In humans, sex is determined by the sex chromosomes. Females have two X chromosomes (XX), and males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY). The mother always contributes an X chromosome; the father contributes either an X or a Y, which determines the sex of the offspring.

questions.stem: Why are X-linked recessive conditions (like colour blindness) more common in males?

options.text: Because males are generally weaker
Because males have only one X chromosome, so one copy of the recessive allele is enough to express the condition — there is no second X to carry a dominant allele
Because the Y chromosome carries the allele for the condition
Because females cannot carry recessive alleles

questions.explanation: Males have only one X chromosome (XY), so if they inherit one copy of an X-linked recessive allele, they will express the condition — there is no second X chromosome to carry a dominant allele that could mask it. Females (XX) would need two copies of the recessive allele to express the condition, making them much less likely to be affected.

questions.stem: What is codominance?

options.text: When one allele completely masks the other
When both alleles are fully expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygote
When a blend of both alleles is expressed
When neither allele is expressed

questions.explanation: In codominance, both alleles are fully expressed simultaneously in the heterozygote. For example, in blood group AB, both the A and B alleles are expressed — the red blood cells carry both A and B antigens. This is different from incomplete dominance, where a blended (intermediate) phenotype is produced.

questions.stem: What is the difference between codominance and incomplete dominance?

options.text: They are the same thing
In codominance, both alleles are fully expressed; in incomplete dominance, a blended/intermediate phenotype is produced
Codominance produces a blend; incomplete dominance shows both traits separately
Codominance only occurs in plants; incomplete dominance only in animals

questions.explanation: In codominance, BOTH alleles are equally and fully expressed (e.g., blood group AB shows both A and B antigens). In incomplete dominance, the phenotype is an INTERMEDIATE blend (e.g., red × white snapdragons → pink). The key difference: codominance = both traits visible; incomplete dominance = blended trait.

questions.stem: Does fertilisation create new alleles?

options.text: Yes — fertilisation produces new alleles
No — fertilisation creates new combinations of existing alleles; only mutations create new alleles
Yes — but only for recessive alleles
No — alleles are destroyed during fertilisation

questions.explanation: Fertilisation creates new COMBINATIONS of alleles (a unique genotype), but it does NOT create new alleles. New alleles can only arise through mutations — changes to the DNA sequence. Fertilisation combines one set of alleles from each parent, giving the offspring a unique combination.

questions.stem: What is an allele?

options.text: A section of DNA that codes for a protein
A different version of a gene
A complete chromosome
A type of mutation

questions.explanation: An allele is a variant form of a gene. Different alleles of the same gene arise through mutations and occupy the same position (locus) on homologous chromosomes. For example, the gene for eye colour may have alleles for brown, blue, or green eyes.

questions.stem: What is cystic fibrosis and how is it inherited?

options.text: A dominant condition — only one copy of the allele is needed
An autosomal recessive condition — two copies of the recessive allele are needed
An X-linked condition that only affects males
A condition caused by having an extra chromosome

questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive condition caused by a mutation in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7. An individual must inherit two copies of the recessive allele (one from each parent) to have the condition. Carriers (heterozygotes) have one copy but do not show symptoms.

questions.stem: Huntington's disease is caused by which type of allele?

options.text: Autosomal recessive
Autosomal dominant
X-linked recessive
Y-linked

questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is caused by an autosomal dominant allele — only ONE copy of the allele is needed to develop the condition. A person who is heterozygous (Hh) will be affected. The condition typically develops in middle age (30-50 years), meaning affected individuals may have already had children before symptoms appear.

questions.stem: What is the expected phenotypic ratio from a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes (Bb × Bb)?
questions.explanation: A monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes (Bb × Bb) produces a 3:1 phenotypic ratio — 3 showing the dominant phenotype (1 BB + 2 Bb) to 1 showing the recessive phenotype (1 bb). The genotypic ratio is 1:2:1 (1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb). The 9:3:3:1 ratio is from a dihybrid cross.

questions.stem: What is the expected phenotypic ratio from a dihybrid cross between two double heterozygotes (BbFf × BbFf)?
questions.explanation: A dihybrid cross between two double heterozygotes produces a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio: 9 showing both dominant traits, 3 showing the first dominant and second recessive, 3 showing the first recessive and second dominant, and 1 showing both recessive traits.

questions.stem: What is the difference between continuous and discontinuous variation?

options.text: There is no difference
Continuous variation shows a range of phenotypes (e.g., height); discontinuous variation shows distinct categories (e.g., blood group)
Continuous variation is genetic; discontinuous variation is environmental
Continuous variation only occurs in plants; discontinuous only in animals

questions.explanation: Continuous variation produces a range of phenotypes with no clear-cut categories (e.g., height, weight, skin colour) — typically controlled by many genes (polygenic) and influenced by environment. Discontinuous variation produces distinct, separate categories (e.g., blood group, attached/free earlobes) — typically controlled by a single gene with little environmental influence.

questions.stem: What is natural selection?

options.text: Humans choosing which organisms to breed
The process where organisms with advantageous traits are more likely to survive, reproduce, and pass on their alleles
Random changes in allele frequency with no direction
The creation of new species by scientists

questions.explanation: Natural selection is the process where individuals with characteristics (phenotypes) better suited to their environment are more likely to survive, reproduce, and pass on the alleles responsible for those characteristics to the next generation. Over time, the frequency of advantageous alleles increases in the population.

questions.stem: What is selective breeding (artificial selection)?

options.text: When organisms naturally choose their mates
When humans choose organisms with desirable traits to breed together, passing those traits to offspring
When organisms adapt to their environment without human help
When genes are artificially inserted into an organism

questions.explanation: Selective breeding (artificial selection) is when humans choose organisms with desirable characteristics and breed them together. Over many generations, the frequency of the desired traits increases. Examples include breeding cows for high milk yield, dogs for specific traits, or wheat for disease resistance.

questions.stem: What is genetic engineering?

options.text: Selective breeding of organisms over many generations
The direct modification of an organism's DNA, often by inserting a gene from another organism
Cloning an organism to produce identical copies
Using X-rays to cause random mutations

questions.explanation: Genetic engineering involves directly modifying an organism's DNA, typically by cutting out a desired gene from one organism (using restriction enzymes) and inserting it into another (using a vector such as a plasmid). The modified organism is called a transgenic or genetically modified organism (GMO). Examples include insulin-producing bacteria and Bt crops.

questions.stem: A carrier of a recessive genetic condition is:

options.text: Homozygous dominant for the condition
Heterozygous — carrying one copy of the recessive allele without showing symptoms
Homozygous recessive and showing all symptoms
Unrelated to the condition

questions.explanation: A carrier is heterozygous — they have one copy of the recessive allele and one copy of the dominant allele. They do not show symptoms (the dominant allele masks the recessive one) but can pass the recessive allele to their offspring. Two carriers have a 25% chance of having an affected child.

questions.stem: What is a mutation?

options.text: A change in the number of chromosomes only
A change in the DNA base sequence of a gene, which may alter the protein produced
A change caused only by radiation
A deliberate change made by genetic engineering

questions.explanation: A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence. This can occur spontaneously during DNA replication or be induced by mutagens (e.g., UV radiation, certain chemicals). Mutations may be harmful, beneficial, or neutral. Most mutations have no effect because the genetic code is degenerate (multiple codons code for the same amino acid).

questions.stem: What is sickle cell disease and how is it inherited?

options.text: An autosomal dominant condition
An autosomal recessive condition — caused by a single base substitution in the haemoglobin gene
An X-linked recessive condition
A condition caused by an extra chromosome

questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive. It is caused by a single base substitution mutation in the gene for haemoglobin, which changes one amino acid (glutamic acid → valine). This causes haemoglobin molecules to form fibres, distorting red blood cells into a sickle shape. Carriers (heterozygotes) have sickle cell trait and some resistance to malaria.

questions.stem: In a pedigree diagram, a horizontal line connecting a male and female represents:

options.text: Siblings
A mating/partnership
Parent and child
Unrelated individuals

questions.explanation: In a pedigree diagram, a horizontal line between a male (square) and female (circle) represents a mating/partnership. A vertical line going down from this connects to their offspring. Siblings are shown connected by a horizontal line above them to the vertical line from their parents.

questions.stem: What evidence supports the theory of evolution by natural selection?

options.text: Only fossil evidence
Fossils, comparative anatomy, DNA/molecular evidence, antibiotic resistance in bacteria, and direct observation of selection
Only DNA evidence
There is no scientific evidence for evolution

questions.explanation: Multiple lines of evidence support evolution: fossil records show changes over time, comparative anatomy reveals homologous structures, DNA/molecular evidence shows relatedness between species, antibiotic resistance in bacteria demonstrates natural selection in action, and scientists have directly observed selection (e.g., Darwin's finches, peppered moths).

questions.stem: What is a clone?

options.text: An organism produced by sexual reproduction
A genetically identical copy of an organism or cell
An organism with a mutation
An organism produced by crossing two different species

questions.explanation: A clone is a genetically identical organism produced by asexual reproduction (e.g., bacterial binary fission, plant vegetative propagation) or artificial cloning techniques (e.g., somatic cell nuclear transfer, as used to create Dolly the sheep). Clones have identical DNA to the parent organism.

questions.stem: What is the phenotypic ratio when a heterozygous organism (Bb) is crossed with a homozygous recessive organism (bb)?

options.text: All dominant

questions.explanation: Bb × bb gives offspring in the ratio 1 Bb : 1 bb, which is a 1:1 phenotypic ratio — 50% showing the dominant phenotype and 50% showing the recessive phenotype. This is the result of a test cross and is used to determine whether an organism showing the dominant phenotype is heterozygous or homozygous.

questions.stem: What is classification?

options.text: The process of creating new species through genetic engineering
The organisation of living organisms into groups based on shared characteristics and evolutionary relationships
The extinction of species over time
The study of fossils

questions.explanation: Classification (taxonomy) is the organisation of living organisms into groups based on shared characteristics. The modern classification system (originally developed by Linnaeus) uses a hierarchy: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. Organisms that share more characteristics are more closely related evolutionarily.

questions.stem: What is the binomial naming system?

options.text: A system where organisms are given a common name only
A system where each species is given a two-part Latin name: Genus (capitalised) and species (lowercase)
A system where organisms are numbered
A system based on where the organism lives

questions.explanation: The binomial system gives each species a unique two-part Latin name: the genus name (capitalised) and the species name (lowercase), both written in italics. For example, Homo sapiens (humans), Panthera leo (lion). This system avoids confusion caused by different common names in different languages.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a gene and an allele?

options.text: They are the same thing
A gene is a section of DNA coding for a protein; an allele is a specific version/variant of that gene
A gene is always dominant; an allele is always recessive
An allele is larger than a gene

questions.explanation: A gene is a section of DNA at a specific locus (position) on a chromosome that codes for a particular polypeptide. An allele is a specific variant of that gene. For example, the gene for eye colour is found at the same locus on a particular chromosome in all humans, but the alleles (versions) of that gene differ, producing different eye colours.

questions.stem: What is a potential disadvantage of selective breeding?

options.text: It increases genetic diversity
It reduces genetic diversity (inbreeding), making populations more vulnerable to disease
It creates new species
It has no disadvantages

questions.explanation: Selective breeding reduces genetic diversity because only organisms with desired traits are bred, narrowing the gene pool. This inbreeding can lead to increased susceptibility to diseases, reduced fertility, and the expression of harmful recessive alleles. If the environment changes, the population may lack the variation needed to adapt.

questions.stem: What is a locus?

options.text: A type of mutation
The specific position of a gene on a chromosome
A type of chromosome
The nucleus of a cell

questions.explanation: A locus (plural: loci) is the specific fixed position on a chromosome where a particular gene is located. Alleles of the same gene occupy the same locus on homologous chromosomes. Knowing the locus of a gene helps in genetic mapping and understanding inheritance patterns.

questions.stem: How can environmental factors influence phenotype?

options.text: Environmental factors cannot influence phenotype — it is entirely genetic
Environmental factors like diet, sunlight, exercise, and temperature can affect how genes are expressed, modifying the phenotype
Environmental factors change the DNA sequence
Environmental factors only affect phenotype in plants, not animals

questions.explanation: Environmental factors can significantly influence phenotype. For example: diet affects height and weight, sunlight affects skin colour, exercise affects muscle mass, and soil pH affects hydrangea flower colour. The phenotype is the result of the interaction between genotype and environment. Identical twins can have different phenotypes due to different environments.

questions.stem: What are restriction enzymes used for in genetic engineering?

options.text: To join DNA fragments together
To cut DNA at specific recognition sequences, often producing sticky ends
To copy DNA during replication
To translate mRNA into protein

questions.explanation: Restriction enzymes (restriction endonucleases) cut DNA at specific short sequences (recognition sites), often producing 'sticky ends' — short single-stranded overhangs that can base-pair with complementary sticky ends from another piece of DNA. This allows the desired gene to be inserted into a vector (e.g., plasmid). DNA ligase then joins the fragments together.

questions.stem: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is an example of which process?

options.text: Selective breeding by humans
Natural selection — bacteria with resistance alleles survive and reproduce, increasing the frequency of resistance in the population
Genetic engineering
Bacteria learning to resist antibiotics during their lifetime

questions.explanation: Antibiotic resistance is a clear example of natural selection in action. Random mutations produce bacteria with resistance alleles. When antibiotics are used, susceptible bacteria die, but resistant ones survive and reproduce, passing on the resistance alleles. Over time, the proportion of resistant bacteria increases. Bacteria do not 'learn' resistance — it arises from random genetic variation.
